# Simulations agree: the Milky Way’s satellites are disrupting

**Authors:** Alexander H. Riley Nora Shipp ††thanks: E-mail: alexander.riley@fysik.lu.se (AHR) Affiliation: Lund Observatory, Division of Astrophysics, Department of Physics, Lund University, SE-221 00 Lund, Sweden Affiliation: Institute for Computational Cosmology, Department of Physics, Durham University, South Road, Durham DH1 3LE, UK J. Sebastian Monzon Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA Arpit Arora Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, Yale University, New Haven, CT 06520, USA Adriana Dropulic Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA Gray Thoron Affiliation: DARK, Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen, Jagtvej 155, 2200 Copenhagen, Denmark Oscar Agertz Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA Santi Roca-Fàbrega Affiliation: Lund Observatory, Division of Astrophysics, Department of Physics, Lund University, SE-221 00 Lund, Sweden Affiliation: Departamento de Física de la Tierra y Astrofísica, Facultad de Ciencias Físicas, Plaza Ciencias, 1, 28040 Madrid, Spain

## Abstract

Recent analyses of simulated Milky Way-mass galaxies have highlighted the prevalence of satellites undergoing tidal disruption. However, these have focused on single hydrodynamical codes with a number of limitations, making it unclear how generic this result is. We compare satellite disruption in four models: two cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (Auriga and FIRE), cosmological $N$ -body simulations with stellar particle tagging (Aquarius), and a semi-analytic model with varying host disk properties (SatGen). For all systems, we compute the fraction of stellar mass retained by the progenitor ( $f_{\text{bound}}$ ) at the present day. We find a remarkable agreement between FIRE, Aquarius, and SatGen; all predict that $\sim$ 20 to 30 per cent of classical-mass satellites have $f_{\text{bound}}<0.9$ ( $\sim$ 5 to 10 per cent have $f_{\text{bound}}<0.5$ ). Satellites in Auriga experience substantially more mass loss than other simulations, which we attribute to their massive central galaxies and large satellite sizes prior to infall. In the ultra-faint regime captured by Aquarius and SatGen, disruption rates are comparable to or exceeding those for classical satellites. The ubiquity of mass loss across models presents both an exciting opportunity (a plethora of stellar streams awaiting discovery) and a nuisance (for theorists using satellite counts to constrain dark matter).

#### Keywords:

## 1 Introduction

Satellite galaxies surrounding Milky Way-mass hosts have been extensively studied in cosmological simulations (Libeskind et al., 2007; Okamoto et al., 2010; Brooks and Zolotov, 2014; Sawala et al., 2016; Wetzel et al., 2016; Applebaum et al., 2021, e.g.,) and semi-analytic models (Kauffmann et al., 1993; Bullock et al., 2000; Benson et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2026; Nadler et al., 2020; Manwadkar and Kravtsov, 2022; Ahvazi et al., 2025) to resolve small-scale challenges to the prevailing $\Lambda$ CDM framework (Sales et al., 2022) or use their observed properties to constrain the nature of dark matter (Nadler et al., 2026). Recent analyses of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations have shown that these satellites are often actively losing stellar mass, forming extended stellar streams (Wang et al., 2017; Panithanpaisal et al., 2021; Riley et al., 2025; Pathak et al., 2025; Meziani et al., 2026). While this may be surprising, given the paucity of tidal tails observed around Milky Way satellites, this debris may be hidden beneath the surface brightness limits of current wide-area photometric surveys (Wang et al., 2017; Shipp et al., 2023).11 1 Detections of clear tidal tails from Antlia II and Crater II (Ji et al., 2021; Atzberger et al., 2026; Limberg et al., 2026) have helped close this gap, but a broad mismatch between simulations and observations remains.

It is unclear to what degree these disruption rates are simply reflecting theoretical limitations, either numerical shortcomings of the simulations or improper physical properties of the satellites. Tailored $N$ -body simulations have highlighted that subhaloes can disrupt artificially due to numerical noise from insufficient number of particles or force resolution (van den Bosch and Ogiya, 2018; Errani and Peñarrubia, 2020; Errani and Navarro, 2021; Chiang et al., 2026; Reddy et al. in prep). Spurious heating due to unequal dark matter and star particle masses can result in galaxies expanding in size (Ludlow et al., 2019; Ludlow et al., 2023; Liao et al. submitted), possibly enhancing disruption upon infall to a larger host. Even beyond these numerical effects, simulated systems that do not follow established scaling relations (e.g., stellar mass-halo mass, stellar mass-size) could experience physical disruption that is nonetheless unrealistic (Peñarrubia et al., 2008; Reddy et al. in prep). On the other hand, many of the careful numerical experiments previously mentioned do not capture physical mechanisms that enhance tidal disruption present in cosmological setups, including preprocessing by massive satellites (He et al., 2025), the tidal field of a growing host with a central disk (Garrison-Kimmel et al., 2017; Kelley et al., 2019; Grand et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2025), and satellite-satellite collisions (Shipp et al., 2025).

These theoretical uncertainties have led to repeated calls to study satellite disruption across a variety of models (Shipp et al., 2023; Shipp et al., 2025, see discussion in). One principled approach to this task could be to analyze disrupting satellites in haloes run with the same initial conditions using different numerical prescriptions, in the spirit of the AGORA comparison project (Kim et al., 2014; Jung et al., 2024). However, this may limit the types of models that can be considered, excluding semi-analytic approaches that are not limited by particle resolution. Another approach is to take a variety of available simulations, with their respective strengths and weaknesses, and invest effort to standardize the analysis as much as possible. If a similar result emerged across methods, this would suggest that the high rate of stellar mass loss is not an effect of one theoretical framework or numerical artefact.

In this work we take the latter approach, comparing disrupting satellites in four different publicly available simulation suites: Auriga, FIRE, Aquarius, and SatGen. These models span a variety of galaxy-halo connections for populating satellites, numerical resolution limitations, and models for enhanced tidal disruption from the host galaxy. In Section 2 we introduce key aspects of the simulation suites and the corresponding catalogues of accreted satellites. In Section 3 we describe how we compute $f_{\text{bound}}$ for the simulations and how we homogenise the merger catalogues. We present our main results in Section 4 and discuss their implications in Section 5.

## 2 Simulations

### 2.1 Auriga

The Auriga simulations (Grand et al., 2017; Grand et al., 2024) are cosmological magnetohydrodynamical zoom simulations of isolated Milky Way-mass galaxies. The haloes were selected from the EAGLE dark-matter-only box (Schaye et al., 2015) to have $M_{\text{200c}}=1-2\times 10^{12}$ M⊙ and satisfy an isolation criterion. They were resimulated using Arepo (Springel, 2010; Pakmor et al., 2016) with a galaxy formation model detailed in Grand et al. (2017); Grand et al. (2024). We use the six Auriga haloes that were simulated at ‘level 3’ resolution, with baryonic element (dark matter particle) masses of $6.7(36)\times 10^{3}$ M⊙ and a minimum softening length of 188 pc. Halo catalogues were constructed using the SUBFIND halo finder (Springel et al., 2001) and connected across time using the LHaloTree merger tree algorithm (Springel et al., 2005).

To identify accreted systems and isolate their constituent star particles, we use the ‘accreted particle lists’ in the Auriga public data release (Grand et al., 2024). To construct these catalogues, star particles are assigned to the (sub)halo they are bound to immediately following their birth. The union of star particles that formed in the main branch of a halo across cosmic time correspond to one system (practically, such particles are assigned the same PeakMassIndex). These are the same catalogues that are used in Riley et al. (2025) and Shipp et al. (2025).

### 2.2 FIRE

We use isolated Milky Way-mass haloes from the Latte suite (Wetzel et al., 2016), run as part of the Feedback in Realistic Environments (FIRE) project. The simulations were run with Gizmo (Hopkins, 2015) using the FIRE-2 galaxy formation model (Hopkins et al., 2018). We use the set of ‘m12’ haloes listed in Table 1 of Wetzel et al. (2023), originally presented across a number of studies (Wetzel et al., 2016; Garrison-Kimmel et al., 2017; Garrison-Kimmel et al., 2019; Hopkins et al., 2018; Samuel et al., 2020). We use seven haloes in total, excluding m12z as its merger catalogue is not available. The haloes were simulated with baryonic (dark matter) mass resolution of $7.1(35)\times 10^{3}$ M⊙22 2 The m12r and m12w haloes were run at slightly worse dark matter resolution of 39,000 $\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ (Samuel et al., 2020). and a softening length of 1 (40) pc. Halo catalogues are produced using the Rockstar algorithm (Behroozi et al., 2013b) and linked into a merger tree using consistent-trees (Behroozi et al., 2013a).

To identify stars in each accretion event, we use catalogues assembled in the same manner as Panithanpaisal et al. (2021). They first construct a list of potential stellar stream candidates by identifying satellites between 2.7 and 6.5 Gyr ago whose star particles are within the host’s $r_{\text{200m}}$ at the present day. To account for satellites that accreted more recently, they augment these catalogues with all present-day satellites (within the host’s $r_{\text{200m}}$ ) that were not accounted for in the previous step. Using the merger trees, they identify the snapshot that each object obtained its maximum stellar mass. They then collect all star particles assigned33 3 When assigning star particles to a halo, Panithanpaisal et al. (2021) select all star particles located within the halo’s virial radius with relative velocities less than twice that halo’s circular velocity curve. to this object for snapshots within a 200 Myr window of this snapshot.

### 2.3 Aquarius

*Figure 1: The stellar mass functions of satellite galaxies across all simulations considered in this work. Shaded contours correspond to the 1 $\sigma$ scatter across haloes, while the solid lines are the medians. For visual clarity, we only show the SatGen scatter for the $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.1$ model, which is similar across disc scenarios. The models span a variety of galaxy-halo connections and host properties, resulting in different stellar mass functions for satellites.*

The Aquarius simulations (Springel et al., 2008) are cosmological zoom simulations of isolated Milky Way-mass haloes. The six haloes were selected from a lower-resolution version of the Millennium-II simulation (Boylan-Kolchin et al., 2009) and resimulated with Gadget-3, an updated version of Gadget-2 (Springel, 2005). To produce stellar distributions for these dark-matter-only simulations, Cooper et al. (2010) used the GALFORM semi-analytic model (Cole et al., 2000; Bower et al., 2006) to model star formation histories for each galaxy and the STINGS particle tagging framework (Cooper et al., 2017; Cooper et al., 2025) to assign stars to dark matter particles (for brevity, we refer to these outputs as ‘Aquarius’). The resulting star particle data were released publicly by Pu et al. (2025).

Cooper et al. (2010) tagged Aquarius haloes that were simulated at ‘level 2’ resolution, with dark matter particle masses ranging from $6.4-14\times 10^{3}$ M⊙ and a softening length of 65.8 pc. Halo catalogues were constructed using the SUBFIND halo finder (Springel et al., 2001) and connected across time using the D-Trees merger tree algorithm (Jiang et al., 2014). Stars formed in a given halo (according to GALFORM) are assigned to that halo’s most tightly bound particles44 4 Cooper et al. (2010) select the most-bound one per cent of particles each snapshot, with stellar mass shared equally among those selected. in the following snapshot. By tracking tagged particles to the present day, accreted stellar haloes comprised of satellites, stellar streams, and phase-mixed debris naturally emerge.

To identify accretion events, we use the progenitor catalogues described in Pu et al. (2025). Star particles that become unbound from a given satellite to join the Milky Way-mass host are assigned the same ProgenitorID. Stars that remain bound to the progenitor at the present day are also assigned that corresponding ID.

### 2.4 SatGen

The SatGen code (Jiang et al., 2021; Green et al., 2021) is a semi-analytic framework to generate statistical samples of satellite galaxy populations. Briefly, SatGen constructs merger trees for dark matter host halos in a given cosmology using the extended Press-Schechter (EPS) method of Parkinson et al. (2008). Once the trees are constructed, SatGen assigns stellar masses (Behroozi et al., 2019, see Appendix J of) and sizes to progenitor halos at accretion and integrates their orbits accounting for dynamical friction and tidal stripping using prescriptions that are calibrated against a large suite of high-resolution idealized simulations.

Throughout the process, SatGen tracks how much stellar mass each satellite loses using tidal tracks defined in Errani et al. (2018) which assume that the ratios stellar mass ( $m_{*}(t)/m_{*}$ ) and stellar size ( $r_{\rm eff}(t)/r_{\rm eff}$ ) can be characterized by

$$ g(x)=\left(\frac{x_{s}+1}{x_{s}+f_{b}}\right)^{\mu}f_{b}^{\eta}\,. $$

Here, $g(x)$ refers to either $m_{*}(t)/m_{*}$ or $r_{\rm eff}(t)/r_{\rm eff}$ , and $f_{b}$ is the instantaneous bound mass fraction of the corresponding dark matter subhalo. The additional parameters $\mu$ , $\eta$ and $x_{s}$ depend on the ‘cuspiness’ of the subhalo at accretion, parameterized by the inner logarithmic slope of the subhalo’s density profile, and on the ratio $r_{\rm eff}/r_{\rm max}$ . Here, $r_{\rm max}$ is the radius at which the subhalo reaches its maximum circular velocity, $v_{\rm max}$ , which for an unevolved NFW density profile is $\sim$ 2.16 $r_{\rm s}$ . SatGen uses a simple interpolation scheme to determine the values of $\mu$ , $\eta$ and $x_{s}$ based on the values inferred by Errani et al. (2018) using a discrete set of simulation results that explored the relevant parameter space.55 5 Since those simulations modeled the stellar bodies as Plummer spheres, we are implicitly assuming the same.

We use merger trees processed in the same manner as in Monzon et al. (2024); Monzon et al. (2026) that fall in a host mass range $M_{\text{vir}}=10^{11.5}-10^{12.5}$ . At every time step we assume that the host’s dark matter potential follows an NFW profile (Navarro et al., 1997). Halo concentrations are computed using the model from Zhao et al. (2009). The galactic disc, when included, is positioned at the centre of the host halo and modeled with the axisymmetric Miyamoto and Nagai (1975) disk that grows with the host (as a constant fraction of the host’s $M_{\text{vir}}$ , see Green et al., 2021). We consider three scenarios: no embedded disc potential, a disc with $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.05$ , and a disc with $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.1$ . Each sample contains 500 unique accretion histories (specifically, a subset of those used in Dropulic et al., 2025) that are identical across the three disc scenarios.

## 3 Methods

### 3.1 Homogenising the merger catalogues

While each of our suites produce catalogues that have comparable contents (a list of accreted systems and their associated star particles), they were not constructed in exactly the same way. To facilitate our $f_{\text{bound}}$ comparison, we apply the following selection criteria to all catalogues:

- 1. Satellite: has a bound component at the present day

- 2. Mass: total stellar mass $M_{\star}>5\times 10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ and bound stellar mass $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}>10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$

- 3. Infall time: fell into the main host within the past 10 Gyr

The first two criteria ensure we are studying surviving classical-mass satellites that are resolved in both Auriga and FIRE. The final one alleviates differences in how far back in time objects need to be tracked. We also consider ultra-faint satellites in Aquarius and SatGen, which capture the tidal evolution of much fainter systems than the hydrodynamical suites. For this, we consider systems with $10^{2}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}<M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}<10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ instead of the mass criteria listed above. We do not apply a selection in distance from the main host.

### 3.2 Bound fractions

*Figure 2: The cumulative distribution of $f_{\text{bound}}$ for classical-mass satellites across different simulation setups. Simulations with satellite systems that are the least disrupted overall will be towards the lower-right corner. We only include systems that have a total stellar mass $M_{\star}>5\times 10^{5}$ M⊙ and a bound stellar mass of $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}>10^{5}$ M⊙. Shaded contours correspond to the 1 $\sigma$ scatter across haloes, while the solid lines are the result considering all systems ‘stacked’. All of the models predict substantial stellar mass loss, with three (FIRE, Aquarius, and SatGen) further agreeing on the amount (within host-to-host scatter).*

Standard halo finders can miss disrupting subhaloes at the resolution typical of zoom simulations (Han et al., 2018; Diemer et al., 2024; Mansfield et al., 2024). To alleviate these concerns, we apply a novel iterative unbinding approach (implemented in nbody_streams; Arora et al., 2026) to both the Auriga and FIRE catalogues. For each snapshot after falling into the main host, we first determine the center of the satellite using a mass-weighted kernel density estimator (KDE) applied to the star particles. The mean position of particles within the highest 1 per cent of the KDE is taken as the initial center. We then compute the potential of the satellite’s dark matter and star particles using a multipole Poisson solver implemented in Agama (Vasiliev, 2019). Particles not bound to this potential are temporarily masked and the potential re-computed, iterating until the number of bound particles changes by less than 0.1 per cent. Satellites are tracked forwards in time until fewer than 5 bound particles remain.

This technique results in modestly larger bound fractions at intermediate stages of disruption ( $0.2<f_{\text{bound}}<0.8$ ) compared to simply relying on the halo finder (see the Appendices of Thoron et al., 2026 for Auriga and Mandacarú Guerra et al., 2026 for FIRE). We note that this method does not compensate for numerical disruption due to low particle count or unequal particle masses (van den Bosch and Ogiya, 2018; Ludlow et al., 2019; Ludlow et al., 2023). If a subhalo disrupts earlier than it should, there is nothing for an improved halo tracker to find.

For the other simulations, $f_{\text{bound}}$ is computed in a more straightforward manner. We assume that the high resolution of Aquarius mitigates concerns of SUBFIND’s ability to track the evolution of subhaloes massive enough to form galaxies.66 6 Santos-Santos et al. (2025); Santos-Santos et al. (2026) raise concerns about the ability of SUBFIND and GALFORM to track the faintest satellites in Aquarius, even at higher resolution than considered here. We remind that satellites with $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}>10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ are the primary focus of this work. Tidal mass loss in SatGen is based on calibrated models (for dark matter) and tidal tracks (for stars), such that identifying the bound remnant is not a concern.

## 4 Results

### 4.1 Stellar mass functions

In Figure 1 we show the stellar mass functions for satellite galaxies across all models considered in this work. These include the iterative unbinding corrections to Auriga and FIRE described in Section 3.2. We intentionally restrict the results from the hydrodynamical simulations (Auriga and FIRE) to $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}>10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ , reflecting their resolution limitations. We caution that the number of satellites is sensitive to host halo mass and assembly history (Boylan-Kolchin et al., 2010; Joshi et al., 2024, e.g.,), and it is not our goal to evaluate how well these predictions compare to observed luminosity functions.

Overall the predictions span a broad range at a given stellar mass, typically over 0.5 dex. Auriga, FIRE, and Aquarius are in reasonable agreement on the typical number of classical satellites ( $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}>10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ ), all falling between 20 to 30. Auriga has the largest number of massive ( $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}>10^{7}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ ) satellites, with far fewer classical satellites below this mass. This reflects the high stellar mass-halo mass relation in Auriga relative to other simulations, particularly for haloes with $M_{\text{peak}}\sim 10^{10}-10^{11}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ , which has been noted in several works (Simpson et al., 2018; Sales et al., 2022; Riley et al., 2025, e.g.,). SatGen predicts fewer classical satellites ( $\sim$ 10-15) than the other simulations, with a modest dependence on the adopted central disk mass. We also note that the SatGen results have larger scatter across all masses than any of the other simulation suites. Given that our SatGen results are based on 500 haloes, we expect this is a more accurate representation of the halo-to-halo scatter for a given model than the more limited samples (6 or 7 haloes) from the other suites.

For ultra-faints ( $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}<10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ ) in Aquarius and SatGen, there is interesting agreement in the cumulative number of satellites within the $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}\sim 10^{3}-10^{4}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ range, but the two profiles exhibit different behavior at higher and lower masses. The SatGen results have a constant slope and the largest number of faint satellites, reflecting the adopted stellar mass-halo mass relation with no cutoff for forming galaxies in the lowest-mass haloes. Comparing versions with different central stellar disks, the strongest reduction in the total number of satellites comes from introducing a disk at all, while doubling the mass of the disk does not have as much of an impact.

Meanwhile, Aquarius exhibits a bimodal distribution of faint and bright satellites, with peaks near $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}\sim 3\times 10^{3}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ and $\sim 3\times 10^{6}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ and a dearth of satellites with $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}\sim 10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ . This is driven by the reionization physics implemented in GALFORM, specifically the parameters that control when reionization takes place and characteristic halo mass scale below which galaxy formation is suppressed (Bose et al., 2018). The suppression of galaxy formation in low-mass haloes results in a divergence between the Aquarius and SatGen counts at the faintest end. We note that the GALFORM model that underpins the Aquarius predictions is a modified version of that presented in Bower et al. (2006) and newer versions of tagged Aquarius haloes with the latest GALFORM parameters produce similar results (Riley et al. in prep).

### 4.2 Bound fractions for classicals

In Figure 2 we present the distribution of $f_{\text{bound}}$ for classical-mass satellites across all of the simulation suites. As we show the cumulative distribution, simulations closer to the lower right corner of the figure ( $f_{\text{bound}}\sim 1$ , $P\sim 0$ ) have the least disrupted satellite populations. For visual clarity, we only show the scatter for the SatGen run with $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.1$ . As supplementary material, we provide a figure that has the same information with simulations shown in separate panels, showing individual hosts (for Auriga, FIRE, and Aquarius) and the scatter for all SatGen models.

The result is striking – most models essentially agree, within their host-to-host scatter, across nearly the full range of disruption (Auriga is the exception, which we discuss in a moment). Between $\sim$ 20 and 30 per cent of satellites have lost at least 10 per cent of their stellar mass ( $f_{\text{bound}}\leq 0.9$ ), while $\sim$ 10 per cent of satellites have lost half or more of their stellar mass ( $f_{\text{bound}}\leq 0.5$ ). This is in spite of FIRE, Aquarius, and SatGen sharing very few modeling choices among all three, beyond grounding their structure formation within a $\Lambda$ CDM cosmology (though with slightly different adopted parameters).

On closer inspection, a number of interesting features emerge. The SatGen models with no stellar disk and $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.05$ are incredibly close to each other, while the $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.1$ model yields the expected result that increasing the stellar disk mass results in more stellar mass loss. The $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.1$ model is also very close to the FIRE result. We note that the present-day $M_{\star}/M_{\text{vir}}$ ratio ranges from 0.05 to 0.09 for FIRE and 0.06 to 0.07 for Auriga, with Auriga disks forming earlier in cosmic time (Belokurov and Kravtsov, 2022). For the Milky Way, this value is likely between 0.02 and 0.05, with uncertainties in both the stellar (Imig et al., 2025; Lian et al., 2025) and dark matter (Wang et al., 2020, e.g.,) components. Aquarius acts as an interesting middle ground between these cases, agreeing with FIRE and the massive SatGen disk results near $f_{\text{bound}}\sim 0.5$ and with the other SatGen models for $f_{\text{bound}}\geq 0.9$ .

The exception to the broad agreement across models is Auriga, which has a much more disrupted satellites. For this suite, $\sim$ 60 per cent of satellites have $f_{\text{bound}}\leq 0.9$ , while nearly 40 per cent of satellites have $f_{\text{bound}}\leq 0.5$ . While previous analysis of Auriga satellites led to the provocative claim that ‘most satellites are streams’ (Riley et al., 2025; Shipp et al., 2025), it is clear that this result is not universal among models. However, while Auriga disagrees with other simulations on the amount of disruption that the Milky Way satellites should be experiencing, it agrees that the disruption is higher than conventionally expected or observationally detected (so far). In Section 5 we discuss potential reasons for this enhanced disruption.

### 4.3 Bound fractions for ultra-faints

*Figure 3: The cumulative distribution of $f_{\text{bound}}$ for ultra-faint satellites, shown in a similar manner as Figure 2. We only include systems that have a bound stellar mass of $10^{2}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}<M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}<10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ . The result for FIRE classical-mass satellites is also shown for comparison. Ultra-faint satellites experience stellar mass loss comparable to, or exceeding, those for classicals.*

In Figure 3 we show the equivalent $f_{\text{bound}}$ distributions for ultra-faint satellites. We only show results for Aquarius and SatGen, which are the models with sufficient numerical resolution and physical prescriptions to analyze satellites with $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}<10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ .

The qualitative trends for ultra-faints are surprisingly similar to those for classicals. The SatGen models with no or lower disk mass are incredibly similar to each other, while the more massive disk model results in a more disrupted satellite population. Aquarius also agrees with the SatGen higher disk mass model for $f_{\text{bound}}\leq 0.7$ and transitions to agree with the other models for $f_{\text{bound}}\geq 0.9$ . The scatter between Aquarius and SatGen are comparable, potentially indicating that improved statistics (many more ultra-faints than classicals) makes the halo-to-halo scatter for $f_{\text{bound}}$ distributions converge with fewer haloes.

Perhaps the most suprising result is that, for a fixed model, the ultra-faints show higher levels of disruption than the classicals. Between $\sim$ 30 and 45 per cent of satellites have $f_{\text{bound}}\leq 0.9$ , while $\sim$ 10 to 20 per cent of satellites have $f_{\text{bound}}\leq 0.5$ . We stress that though Aquarius and SatGen have different galaxy-halo connections resulting in quite different predictions for the total number of ultra-faints (Figure 1), their $f_{\text{bound}}$ distributions are much more similar.

## 5 Discussion and concluding remarks

It has been widely noted that satellites in cosmological (typically hydrodynamical) simulations are experiencing tidal disruption, even invoking this as a mechanism to alleviate small-scale problems of $\Lambda$ CDM (Brooks and Zolotov, 2014; Wetzel et al., 2016; Fattahi et al., 2018). Several studies using controlled experiments have claimed that such results are subject to numerical effects (van den Bosch and Ogiya, 2018; Ludlow et al., 2019; Ludlow et al., 2023; Errani and Navarro, 2021; Chiang et al., 2026) and that the results from hydrodynamical simulations in particular should be treated with caution.

Our baseline result -- that several models and methodologies all produce disrupting satellite populations -- is a substantial deviation from this conventional wisdom. It is worth noting the numerical strengths and weaknesses of each simulation in turn.77 7 We necessarily are painting with a broad brush, without commenting on whether these weaknesses are dealbreakers (or if the strengths are sufficient) in the context of disrupting satellites. Auriga and FIRE are likely most impacted by particle resolution and spurious heating, but include ‘messy’ cosmological effects like a turbulent assembly history and satellite-satellite interactions. Aquarius is not subject to spurious heating and is higher resolution than Auriga and FIRE, but does not include additional disruption due to a central stellar disk. SatGen does not suffer from numerical noise and can include the growth of a host disk (in a relatively simplified manner), but does not capture satellite-satellite interactions. Despite this mixture of strengths and weaknesses, three of these models (FIRE, Aquarius, SatGen) not only qualitatively agree that their satellites have experienced disruption, but on the degree of that disruption.

The remaining model (Auriga) predicts a substantially higher level of disruption than the others. As noted in Section 4, the stellar mass-halo mass relation for Auriga satellites is higher than comparable simulations and observational constraints (see Section 6.4 of Riley et al., 2025 for a summary). Low-mass field galaxies in Auriga are also larger than observations at a fixed stellar mass, particularly for $M_{\star}<10^{8}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ (Bose et al., 2019, e.g., Figure 1 of). The Auriga central galaxies also mostly fall above the the typical $M_{\star}-M_{\text{200c}}$ relation (Fragkoudi et al., 2025, e.g., Figure 10 of). Taken together, this means that the typical $\sim$ $10^{10}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$ halo is populated with a more massive and more extended galaxy (larger satellites lose stellar mass more readily; Reddy et al. in prep), then falls onto the main Auriga host to evolve in a stronger tidal field. This combination could provide a physical explanation of the enhanced disruption relative to FIRE, even though the two share many of the same potential numerical effects.

It is worth considering that both Aquarius and SatGen find that ultra-faints are more disrupted than classicals. Efforts to model Milky Way satellites typically assign stellar masses (or luminosities) to subhaloes based on their peak halo mass, then assume that this mass does not change unless the satellite is fully disrupted and removed from the sample (Nadler et al., 2020; Manwadkar and Kravtsov, 2022; Ahvazi et al., 2025, e.g.,). This decision is typically justified by comparing notes with high-resolution numerical experiments. However, we note that the tidal tracks used in SatGen are calibrated to similar results (Errani et al., 2018), suggesting that substantial stellar mass loss is entirely possible with such frameworks. We encourage such efforts to not only consider increases in galaxy size from tidal heating (which are typically implemented), but also stellar mass loss in their forward modeling.

Stellar mass loss of ultra-faints has been relatively unexplored, since these systems are difficult to model in a Milky Way-like environment. Taking the most conservative of these models (SatGen with no disk) implies that of the 33 spectroscopically-confirmed ultra-faint galaxies discovered to date (Pace, 2025), on average $\sim$ 10 have lost 10 per cent of their stellar mass and $\sim$ 3 have lost over half of their stellar mass. Meanwhile, only Tucana III exhibits clearly detected tidal tails (Li et al., 2018), while claims surrounding Boötes III’s tidal tails (Carlin and Sand, 2018; Jensen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) and nature as a galaxy or star cluster (Zaremba et al., 2025; Cerny et al., 2026) are disputed. If these models are correct, many ultra-faints have tidal tails yet undetected. Recent detections (Jensen et al., 2024) of extended stellar distributions surrounding 7 Milky Way ultra-faint satellites (including Boötes III and Tucana III) may be an encouraging sign. We note that diagnostics of disruption used in the literature (e.g., shape, size, proper motion alignment) may be unreliable indicators of a satellite’s present-day disruption state (Thoron et al., 2026).

We close on the following – a variety of theoretical models predicting tidal disruption does not mean that these predictions reflect reality. It is even possible that the recently unravelled debris could be at such a low surface brightness to never be detectable, even with upcoming facilities including NSF-DOE Rubin, Euclid, Roman, and Arrakihs. Detailed mock observations, in both the resolved star (Shipp et al., 2023) and integrated light (Miró-Carretero et al., 2025) regimes, will play a crucial role in determining if satellite disruption rates in the Milky Way and external galaxies are consistent with these models. It is even possible that all of these models are wrong, requiring either new numerical prescriptions or even new physics that shield satellites from forming tidal streams and other debris. However, the alternative is thrilling – an abundance of low surface brightness tidal substructures that will reveal itself within the next decade, if galactic archeologists search for it.

# StreamGen: Connecting Populations of Streams and Shells to Their Host Galaxies

**Authors:** Adriana Dropulic Affiliation: Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Corresponding author: Adriana Dropulic Nora Shipp Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA Stacy Kim Affiliation: Carnegie Observatories, 813 Santa Barbara Street, Pasadena, CA 91101, USA Zeineb Mezghanni Affiliation: Department of Physics, Grinnell College, Guildford, Grinnell, IA 50112, USA Lina Necib Affiliation: Department of Physics and Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, MIT, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Affiliation: The NSF AI Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Mariangela Lisanti Affiliation: Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Affiliation: Center for Computational Astrophysics, Flatiron Institute, 162 Fifth Ave, New York, NY 10010, USA

## Abstract

In this work, we study how the abundance and dynamics of populations of disrupting satellite galaxies change systematically as a function of host galaxy properties. We apply a theoretical model of the phase-mixing process to classify intact satellite galaxies, stellar stream-like and shell-like debris in ${\sim}\,1500$ Milky Way-mass systems generated by a semi-analytic galaxy formation code, SatGen. In particular, we test the effect of host galaxy halo mass, disk mass, ratio of disk scale height to length, and stellar feedback model on disrupting satellite populations. We find that the counts of tidal debris are consistent across all host galaxy models, within a given host mass range, and that all models can have stream-like debris on low-energy orbits, consistent with those observed around the Milky Way. However, we find a preference for stream-like debris on lower-energy orbits in models with a thicker (lower-density) host disk or on higher-energy orbits in models with a more-massive host disk. Importantly, we observe significant halo-to-halo variance across all models. These results highlight the importance of simulating and observing large samples of Milky Way-mass galaxies and accounting for variations in host properties when using disrupting satellites in studies of near-field cosmology.

## I Introduction

In the $\Lambda$ Cold Dark Matter ( $\Lambda$ CDM) paradigm, galaxies form through the process of hierarchical structure formation [128], accumulating mass though the accretion and disruption of other, smaller galaxies. Observational signatures of this process include largely intact satellite galaxies, like the Milky Way’s LMC [103], as well as the luminous remnants of satellite galaxies tidally disrupted by the host’s gravitational potential; for reviews, see [51, 11]. This debris falls broadly into two morphological categories: stream-like debris, which are coherent structures of tidally stripped stars that roughly follow their progenitor’s orbit, and shell-like debris, which are more phase-mixed structures that form concentric arcs of stars perpendicular to their progenitor’s orbit.

Recent observations of surviving satellite galaxy populations, in the Milky Way and in external galaxies, have provided critical insight into the properties of dark matter and the processes involved in small-scale galaxy formation; for a review, see [19]. These observations have produced some of the the strongest constraints on galaxy formation at small scales and the properties of dark matter, but also revealed questions, including the missing satellites [87, 69], core-cusp [91], too-big-to-fail (TBTF) [13, 14, 12], and the plane-of-satellites [93, 71] problems. A partial resolution to the remaining questions has been achieved by modifying cosmological simulations to include baryonic physics [127, 43, 40, 115, 18, 67, 44, 107]. Tidal stripping of satellites is a critical component of this resolution, as it reduces the number of satellites and their central densities [135, 15, 17, 43, 44], yet it is a large source of uncertainty—numerically, theoretically, and observationally—in various studies [122, 121, 20, 37]. The study of tidal disruption is additionally important because theories of dark matter and galaxy evolution can be constrained by tidal disruption rates [94, 38, 36]. This is because the tidal disruption of satellite galaxies is highly sensitive to their underlying density profiles, which are in turn influenced by the particle nature of dark matter [29, 120, 65, 31, 111] and baryonic physics [44]. It is therefore essential to gain a more complete understanding of tidal stripping and satellite disruption—throughout entire halos of galaxies and at all stages of tidal disruption—through observation, theoretical modeling, and simulation.

The study of debris structures has become possible with observational and theoretical advances in detecting and modelling stripped satellites. The recent discoveries of numerous streams in the Milky Way [112, 75, 81, 85, e.g.] and several candidates in external galaxies [82, 23, 88, 64, e.g.] have opened the opportunity for studying the disruption rate of satellite galaxies. Further, there is evidence of shell-like structures in the Galaxy [52, 25, 28] and in other galaxies [83, 30, 8, 27, for example,]. However, until recently, there has not been a straightforward description of the conditions that cause tidal debris to form a shell rather than a stream. Massive, radial mergers have been shown to preferentially produce shell-like debris in simulations [2, 101, 66]. [2] derived key parameters and mechanisms that dictate the morphology of tidal stream-like debris, including the mass ratio of merging galaxies, orbital parameters, dynamical friction, accretion time, and host galaxy potential. Later, [53] crucially connected the formation of stream-like debris to that of shell-like debris through a theoretical model of the phase-mixing process as a function of the merging satellites’s mass, orbit, and interaction time, as well as the host galaxy’s properties.

Significant advances in modeling tidal debris have also been made in cosmological hydrodynamical simulations [54, 55, 56, 45, 1, 3, e.g.,] that have provided unprecedented insight into stream formation [92, 5, 114, Riley et al. 2024 in prep., Shipp et al. 2024 in prep.]. [114] identified populations of detectable stream-like debris in the Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE) simulations [54, 55] and found a potential discrepancy between simulations and observations—the stream-like debris identified in 13 Milky Way analogs consistently have higher pericenters and apocenters than the Milky Way stream-like debris. This disagreement could be due to any property that affects the tidal disruption of satellites, for example the host galaxy’s properties (such as its total mass and structure), the implementation of baryonic feedback, the resolution of the simulations, or the dark matter physics. For example, it has been shown in the literature that host properties, such as disk and halo mass, can have significant impact on satellite survivability, diversity, and orbits [43, 60], and will thus necessarily impact the population of stream-like debris and shell-like debris.

However, the cosmological hydrodynamical simulations that investigate these questions about satellite tidal disruption are computationally expensive, making it challenging to disentangle the effects of various factors on the tidal debris population, including subgrid modeling in the simulations, the assumed dark matter model, and halo-to-halo variance. These systematics may cause the differences between observations and simulations of the Milky Way, which could be misinterpreted as small-scale structure discrepancies with $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$ . Sophisticated models that generate populations of stream-like and shell-like debris are crucial for fully understanding how host galaxy properties influence tidal disruption.

Semi-analytic tools are an efficient way to rapidly generate multiple realizations of disrupted satellite populations, varying host properties [70, 76, 80, 50, 41, 7, 16, 117, 6, 102, 49, 78, 61, 89, 131, 60, 90]. In this work, we extend SatGen, a semi-analytical satellite galaxy generator that can efficiently produce satellite populations for a large number of host halos [60]. We evolve each satellite in the dynamic potential of the host and apply a theoretical model of phase mixing to each satellite’s orbit to estimate whether it is intact or if its debris would be stream-like or shell-like. These broad steps comprise a debris identification pipeline for satellite galaxies, which we call StreamGen. The pipeline is based on an analytic model by Hendel & Johnston [53] (hereafter HJ15), which describes how satellites phase mix over time. We apply the “morphology metric” from HJ15 to the SatGen satellite orbits to generate stream-like and shell-like tidal debris populations in ${\sim}\,1500$ Milky Way-mass galaxies. We vary the host’s mass, disk mass, and disk height around current best estimates of Milky Way values. For a given mass range of host galaxy, we find that the variations in disk properties that we selected do not significantly affect the orbital properties of stream and shell populations, especially when compared to halo-to-halo variance.

This paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces StreamGen, our debris morphology identification code, including a brief overview of the initial SatGen satellite galaxy generator and our extension to it to predict which satellites turn into stream-like or shell-like debris based on our implementation of the HJ15 morphology metric. Section III uses the results from StreamGen to demonstrate how stream-like and shell-like populations vary across Milky Way-mass galaxies with varying properties. In Section III.1, we present the fiducial model, and in Section III.2, we explore the effect of host halo and disk properties, as well as stellar feedback models, on stream-like and shell-like populations. We conclude in Sec. IV with a discussion comparing our results to stream populations in cosmological simulations and a discussion of future work in light of upcoming surveys. Appendix A describes the effect of uncertainty in the morphology metric assignment on our results. Appendix B contains additional plots of potential interest to the reader.

Our debris identification code, StreamGen, which is built to classify tidal debris populations in SatGen, but in principle could be applied to the outputs from any other satellite generator, is available on GitHub.

## II Simulations

In this section, we detail the steps required to generate populations of tidal debris structures from a semi-analytical satellite generator. Section II.1 reviews the generation of merger trees as well as the choice of a subhalo’s initial conditions and its subsequent orbital evolution, as modeled by SatGen. Section II.2 discusses the definition of a morphology metric as the basis for identifying stream-like and shell-like debris given a satellite’s properties. Section II.3 presents the implementation of this model for SatGen, which we call StreamGen. Section II.5 validates StreamGen using N-body simulations.

### II.1 SatGen

[60] presents SatGen, a semi-analytic model of subhalo evolution within a host halo. The semi-analytic nature of the model permits the efficient generation of a large statistical sample of galaxies and their subhalos. A goal of this work is to classify what these subhalos look like at redshift $z=0$ : whether they remain largely intact or if they have tidal debris that is predominantly stream-like or shell-like. SatGen has a variety of tuneable properties that can emulate different cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, such as the structure of the host galaxy and the strength of stellar feedback, which can affect tidal disruption of satellites. These properties and the selections used in this work are described in this section.

SatGen creates satellite populations in a two-step process: it generates halo merger trees and subsequently evolves satellite orbit and structure. In SatGen, the halo merger trees are generated using an algorithm based on the extended Press-Schechter (EPS) formalism [73]. Given a target halo of known mass and redshift, EPS gives the expected number and mass of progenitor halos at any earlier redshift. Using the EPS formalism allows for the rapid random sampling of assembly histories, which is useful for studying halo-to-halo variance [60]. The host mass is given by the merger tree branch that tracks the most massive progenitor. The mass of the disk is a user-specified fraction of the host mass; [60] note that these disks mimic, but do not reproduce, the Milky Way’s disk and are similar to the disks in the simulations of [96].

After the merger trees are defined, the orbits and baryonic properties of satellites are initialized. Orbits of satellite galaxies are modeled based on distributions motivated by cosmological simulations [77], which find that infall velocities of satellites follow a nearly-universal distribution peaking near the host’s virial velocity.11 1 We note that the results of this work could be sensitive to the infall velocity distribution, which is in turn dependent on the cosmology, but we did not explicitly examine this in this work. Properties such as the stellar mass and stellar size are assigned to subhalos at infall using the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SMHM), assuming a scatter of 0.15 dex in $M_{*}$ at a given $M_{\mathrm{vir}}$ [106]. We note that observations of nearby satellite systems indicate this may significantly underestimate the scatter in the SMHM relation in subhalos with $M_{\mathrm{vir}}\lesssim 10^{11}M_{\odot}$ [e.g. 24, and references therein], which would affect subhalo evolution. The stellar half-mass radius is evolved without assuming an underlying density profile for the stars [59].

SatGen can emulate the baryonic feedback of the Numerical Investigation of Hundred Astrophysical Objects (NIHAO) simulations [118, 42], which is characterized by repeated, short bursts of star formation. It can also emulate the feedback of the A Project Of Simulating The Local Environment (APOSTLE) simulations [110], which has a smoother progression of star formation. The “bursty” feedback of the NIHAO simulations can simultaneously make dwarf galaxies more puffy and centrally cored [33], causing them to be more susceptible to tidal disruption. The “smooth” feedback of the APOSTLE simulations does not significantly core dwarf galaxies and therefore leaves them more resistant to tidal disruption. SatGen’s halo response to star formation and feedback, which affects the tidal disruption of satellites, is implemented through a numerical correction to the subhalo’s concentration and its inner density slope before satellite infall, as derived from the respective hydrodynamical simulation; this is described in Sec. III.2.3.

In this work, all SatGen halos have a Dekel-Zhao profile [26, 42]. The Dekel-Zhao density profile is presented as a function of ${x\equiv r/r_{\mathrm{s}}}$ , where $r$ is the galactocentric radius and ${r_{\mathrm{s}}=r_{\mathrm{vir}}/c}$ is the scale radius, which is defined in terms of the concentration $c$ and virial radius $r_{\text{vir}}$ . The Dekel-Zhao density profile is given by

$$ \rho(x)=\frac{\rho_{0}}{x^{\alpha}\left(1+x^{1/\beta}\right)^{\beta(\gamma-\alpha)}}\,, $$

where $\beta=2$ is chosen in SatGen, ${\gamma=3+\beta^{-1}=3.5}$ , ${\alpha=-\mathrm{dln}\rho/\left.\mathrm{dln}r\right|_{r\rightarrow 0}}$ is the (negative of the) logarithmic density slope in the halo center. The numerator is given by ${\rho_{0}=\left[c^{3}(1-\alpha/3)/f(c,\alpha)\right]\Delta_{c}\varrho_{\mathrm{crit}}}$ with ${f(x,\alpha)=\chi(x)^{2(3-\alpha)}}$ and ${\chi(x)\equiv x^{1/2}/\left(1+x^{1/2}\right)}$ . $\varrho_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is the critical density and $\Delta_{c}$ is the spherical overdensity with respect to the critical density. Additionally, galactic disks are described by the profile in [86], hereafter the MN profile. An MN disk is defined using three parameters: the disk mass, $M_{d}$ , a scale radius, $a$ , and a scale height, $b$ . Its density profile is given by

$$ \rho(R,z)=\frac{M_{\mathrm{d}}b^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{aR^{2}+(a+3\zeta)(a+\zeta)^{2}}{\zeta^{3}\left[R^{2}+(a+\zeta)^{2}\right]^{5/2}}, $$

where $\zeta=\sqrt{z^{2}+b^{2}}$ and $R$ , $\phi$ , and $z$ are the cylindrical coordinates.

SatGen evolves a satellite’s orbit as well as its structure within the host, including dynamical friction [21], tidal effects [47], and density-profile evolution [46, via a transfer function;]. In particular, two competing effects—tidal stripping and tidal heating—are dominant contributions to the evolution of satellite mass and structure. While tidal stripping reduces the size of a satellite by removing mass, tidal heating causes the satellite to expand by increasing its internal kinetic energy. The total mass loss to tides is given by

$$ dm=\alpha_{se}[m-m(r_{\mathrm{tide}})]\frac{dt}{t_{\mathrm{dyn}}}\,, $$

where $\alpha_{se}$ is the stripping efficiency parameter, $m$ is the satellite’s peak mass, $r_{\mathrm{tide}}$ is the satellite tidal radius, $dt$ is a timestep, and $t_{\mathrm{dyn}}$ is the host dynamical time at the satellite position. The host dynamical time is given by

$$ t_{\mathrm{dyn}}(r)=\sqrt{\frac{3\pi}{16G\bar{\rho}(r)}}\,, $$

where $G$ is the universal gravitational constant and $\bar{\rho}(r)$ is the average density of the host at the satellite position.

The analytic description of a satellite’s net structural change is complicated because the effect of tidal heating must be considered in tandem with that of tidal stripping. To this end, tidal-evolution tracks, obtained from numerical simulations, are used to evolve subhalo density profiles as well as stellar masses and half-mass radii [96, 39, 35]. Qualitatively, a satellite’s size initially increases with subhalo mass loss due to tidal heating and re-virialization and then decreases as stripping becomes more dominant [60]. The tidal tracks were verified by [35] to be consistent with high-resolution N-body simulations down to $M(r<r_{\mathrm{mx}})/M_{\mathrm{acc}}(r<r_{\mathrm{mx}})\approx 1/300$ , where $r_{\mathrm{mx}}\approx 2.16r_{s}$ , $r_{s}$ is the scale radius of the halo, and $M_{\mathrm{acc}}$ indicates the subhalo mass at accretion.

The workflow described in this section can produce populations of satellites and their disruption rates around a range of Milky Way-like hosts. It is important to note a few limitations of the current SatGen model, including that it assumes spherical symmetry for the host and satellites and does not model a few processes: the disk growth (except as a function of the total virial mass of the host) or dynamics, the back reaction of the satellites on the host halo, and the interaction of satellites with each other. These processes will complicate the tidal disruption process and present an avenue for future development.

### II.2 Morphology Metric

HJ15 developed a method to classify tidal debris based on their orbital properties. HJ15 introduces a “morphology metric” that quantifies the conditions required for stream-like and shell-like structures to form in terms of the satellite’s mass, orbit, and interaction time, leveraging scaling relations that govern orbital debris evolution and a simple model of how orbits phase mix over time. This allows us to approximate whether tidal debris is stream-like or shell-like. HJ15 recognized that debris structures span a spectrum of morphologies from streams to shells, including a few structures that possess qualities of both (i.e. their “umbrella” systems) or are difficult to classify by eye. As such, we use the terminology “stream-like” and “shell-like” to denote this uncertainty. This section will describe the morphology metric as defined in HJ15; the implementation for SatGen will be described in Sec. II.3.

A variety of factors determine the shape and properties of a satellite galaxy’s orbit: the total orbital energy ( $E_{\rm orb}$ ), total orbital angular momentum ( $L_{\rm orb}$ ), the host potential, the radii of the orbit at apocenter ( $r_{\mathrm{apo}}$ ) and pericenter ( $r_{\mathrm{peri}}$ ), the radial orbital period ( $T_{r}$ ), the precession per orbit between successive apocenters ( $\Delta\psi$ ) (referred to simply as the “precession angle”), and the angular “width” of a single rosette petal of the orbit ( $\alpha_{r}$ ). Alternatively, $\alpha_{r}$ is the angle through which the particle moves during the outer half of its radial period. Figure 1 shows the orbits of two disrupting SatGen satellite galaxies, in blue and orange, which will be discussed in detail later in this section. For illustrative purposes at this point, the angles $\Delta\psi$ and $\alpha_{r}$ are shown in projection for the SatGen satellite orbit in the top panel of Fig. 1.

*Figure 1: Orbits of two satellite galaxies in SatGen that are identified by the morphology metric as stream-like (blue) and shell-like (orange). The dark, solid line is the original SatGen orbit from satellite accretion until the point at which the morphology metric is calculated, which is 8.6 (4.8) Gyr for the stream (shell). The light-to-dark gradient of this line indicates the time progression of the orbit from accretion until the point where the satellite has lost all but $1/300$ of its total initial mass. The thin lines in the background are the orbits of the “stars” sampled from the SatGen satellite’s velocity dispersion and forward integrated from the point at which the morphology is calculated in the static host potential. The labels in the top panel correspond to the angle between apocenters ( $\Delta\psi$ ) in grey and the rosette petal angle ( $\alpha_{r}$ ) in black.*

The energy ( $E$ ) and angular momentum ( $L$ ) dispersions for tidal debris are typically set at a satellite’s pericenter, where satellite usually loses the most mass. In the HJ15 model, particles become unbound from the satellite through points approximately located at the satellite’s (satellite-centric) tidal radius ( $r_{\mathrm{tide}}$ ):

$$ r_{\mathrm{tide}}=\left(\frac{m}{3M(r_{\mathrm{peri}})}\right)^{1/3}r_{\mathrm{peri}}\,, $$

where $m$ is the satellite’s total dark matter mass at infall, and $M(r_{\mathrm{peri}})$ is the enclosed host mass at $r_{\mathrm{peri}}$ .

The difference in the host galaxy’s gravitational potential energy across the satellite at pericenter determines the energy scale of the debris,

$$ e_{s}=2r_{\mathrm{tide}}\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial r}\bigg|_{r_{\mathrm{peri}}}\,, $$

where $\Phi$ is the host potential.

The angular momentum scale is given by

$$ l_{s}=(\sqrt{3}+2)\left(\frac{m}{3M(r_{\mathrm{peri}})}\right)^{1/3}L_{\rm orb}. $$

The angular spread of debris due to differences in azimuthal precession over time, $\Psi_{L}$ , is given by

$$ \Psi_{L}=l_{s}N_{\rm orb}\frac{\partial\Delta\psi}{\partial L}\bigg|_{E_{\rm orb}}, $$

where $N_{\rm orb}$ is the number of orbits.

Stream-like variations in orbital period generate the angle $\Psi_{E}$ , which is given by

$$ \Psi_{E}=e_{s}N_{\rm orb}\frac{\Delta\psi}{T_{r}}\frac{\partial T_{r}}{\partial E}\bigg|_{L_{\rm orb}}. $$

$\Psi_{E}$ is restricted to be less than $\alpha_{r}$ so that only individual rosette petals are considered. The morphology metric is therefore defined as

$$ \mu\equiv\bigg|\frac{\Psi_{L}}{\Psi^{1}_{E}}\bigg|\,, $$

where

$$ \Psi^{1}_{E}\equiv\text{min}(\alpha_{r},\Psi_{E}). $$

For dynamically-young debris, $\Psi^{1}_{E}>\Psi_{L}$ . Eventually, $\Psi^{1}_{E}$ would become greater than $\alpha_{r}$ , so when $\Psi^{1}_{E}=\alpha_{r}$ , $\Psi^{1}_{E}$ remains constant at $\alpha_{r}$ thereafter. As the precession angle increases, angular momentum effects have a greater impact on the morphology. This continues until $\Psi_{L}=\Psi^{1}_{E}$ , at which point the merger results in the formation of a shell-like structure. A faster transition occurs for higher-mass satellites.

### II.3 StreamGen

In this section, we present our implementation of the morphology metric in SatGen, which we call StreamGen. We explain how all inputs into the morphology metric, discussed in Sec. II.2, are calculated and examine the orbits, mass loss, and corresponding morphology metric values of two SatGen satellite galaxies. Importantly, we consider satellites that have $M_{*}>5\times 10^{5}~M_{\odot}$ at accretion and do not fall within 4 kpc of the center of the primary host.22 2 We do this to eliminate satellites whose orbits are susceptible to numerical effects at small radii $\lesssim 4$ kpc, as we find that as the satellite-host distance becomes small, the $1/r^{2}$ force can artificially kick the satellite out of the host. The radial resolution is 0.01 kpc, after which the satellite is considered to have merged fully into the host.

If a satellite has lost less than $10\%$ of its total stellar mass by $z=0$ , it is considered to be intact. For satellites which have lost more mass and are considered disrupted, we calculate the morphology metric at satellite pericenter, as this is where most debris stripping occurs. We select the pericenter just preceding the point when the satellite has lost all but 1/300 of the dark matter mass within its virial radius,33 3 We choose this point as an approximation to the limit to which [35]’s tidal tracks have been validated with simulations, which is down to 1/300 of the initial (pre-infall) mass within $r_{\rm mx}$ . As mass loss is more severe in the outskirts, our cut on 1/300 of the mass left within the virial radius rather than $r_{\rm mx}$ is conservative. at which point a significant fraction of the stars will have been stripped; hereafter, we refer to this point as “p300.” We assume that the orbit of the remnant satellite at p300 well approximates the morphology of the stellar debris. If the satellite does not reach p300, the morphology metric assignment occurs at the most recent pericenter. The time between p300 and the most recent pericenter can vary depending on multiple factors such as satellite mass, initial merger configuration, and accretion time. We estimate the morphology of the stellar debris by applying the morphology metric at p300. In general, at this point, satellites can still retain $\sim 50\%$ of their stellar mass, which means that we are likely probing the morphology of this debris as it is stripped. This point is also significant because after the satellite has lost a greater fraction of its mass than it has at p300, the tidal tracks have not been explicitly validated against N-body simulations, although they still reproduce results from N-body simulations well [35].

Next, we discuss the inputs to the morphology metric that are calculated at p300 or most recent pericenter, according to the paragraph above. To calculate the derivative quantities in $\Psi_{L}$ and $\Psi_{E}$ in the morphology metric, 300--1000 particles are sampled44 4 We sample 1000 times if a satellite’s $r_{\mathrm{peri}}<20$ kpc and $r_{\mathrm{apo}}<50$ kpc, suggesting that it is more likely to be disrupted. The sampling rate is set by requiring that the calculated derivative quantities are stable. from the SatGen satellite’s velocity dispersion, $\sigma$ :

$$ \sigma^{2}(x)=\frac{2V_{\mathrm{vir}}^{2}c}{f(c,\alpha)}\frac{x^{3.5}}{\chi^{2(3.5-\alpha)}}\sum_{i=0}^{i=8}\frac{(-1)^{i}8!(1-\chi^{4(1-\alpha)+i})}{i!(8-i)!(4(1-\alpha)+i)}\,, $$

where $V_{\mathrm{vir}}$ is the virial velocity, and the other quantities are as defined for Eq. 1. Eq. 12 is derived from [134] (which follows [119]). As this is $\sigma$ for a 1D velocity dispersion, assuming spherical symmetry and time independence, we take $\sigma$ to be the velocity dispersion in each Cartesian direction.55 5 We do not consider anisotropy of the velocity dispersion, as we only utilize the sampling step to get an estimate of the derivative of orbital quantities, in Eq. 8 and Eq. 9, calculated from the sampled particles. Each particle is then drawn from the multivariate Gaussian distribution where the dispersion is given by Eq. 12 and the mean is given by the satellite’s average velocity in SatGen.

To obtain orbits and orbital quantities of the sampled particles for the morphology assignment procedure, we evolve the particles for 2–3 orbital periods in the host potential at the time of p300. The total orbital energy is calculated as $E_{\rm orb}=\Phi(r_{\mathrm{peri}})+\frac{1}{2}v_{p}^{2}$ , and the orbital angular momentum is $L_{\rm orb}=|\bf{r}_{\mathrm{peri}}\times\bf{v}_{p}|$ at first pericenter, where $\bf{v}_{p}$ is the satellite velocity at pericenter. The precession per orbit, $\Delta\psi$ , between successive apocenters, $\bf{r}_{\rm apo,1}$ and $\bf{r}_{\rm apo,2}$ , is calculated as

$$ \Delta\psi=2\pi-\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\bf{r}_{\rm apo,1}\cdot\bf{r}_{\rm apo,2}}{|\bf{r}_{\rm apo,1}||\bf{r}_{\rm apo,2}|}\right)\,, $$

where the $2\pi$ is necessary for the metric to be a positive value as in HJ15. $\Delta\Psi$ is illustrated in Fig. 1. Finally, the radial orbital period, $T_{r}$ , is calculated as the time between consecutive apocenters, ${t_{\bf{r}_{\rm apo,1}}-t_{\bf{r}_{\rm apo,2}}}$ . To calculate the derivative quantities in the morphology metric, in Eq. 8 and Eq. 9, we evaluate the slope of $\Delta\psi$ versus $L$ of particles at the $E_{\rm orb}$ of the original SatGen satellite. Similarly, we evaluate the slope of $T_{r}$ versus $E$ of particles at the $L_{\rm orb}$ of the original SatGen satellite. These values are input into the morphology metric described in Sec. II.2 to classify SatGen debris as stream-like or shell-like.

*Figure 2: Mass loss for dark matter (solid lines) and stars (dashed lines) over time for the satellites with stream-like debris (blue) and shell-like debris (orange) shown in Fig. 1. At points where the stellar mass loss is above the dotted grey line (i.e. $M_{*}/M_{*,\mathrm{z_{acc}}}=0.9$ ), satellites are considered to be intact. The dashed-dotted grey line denotes “p300,” the point where the satellite has lost all but $1/300$ of its total initial mass. The pericenter closest to this intersection is where the morphology metric is calculated in this analysis. If a satellite does not reach this point, its morphology is calculated at most recent pericenter.*

There are several key differences between the simulations HJ15 used to define the morphology metric and SatGen. In particular, HJ15’s morphology metric is defined by the dark matter properties of the satellite and focuses on satellite orbital properties; it does not directly account for the internal properties of the satellite. HJ15 does approximate the effect of stripping dark matter before stars by using $20\%$ of the initial satellite mass in the metric calculation, Eq. 10. Additionally, HJ15’s morphology metric does not correct for dynamical friction and the variation in tidal radius as the satellite orbits. Dynamical friction and the tidal radius modeling are included in SatGen and are therefore intrinsically included in the morphology metric for StreamGen. On the other hand, SatGen does not track the location of the lost mass; it only reports the location of the satellite in the halo and its mass at each timestep. SatGen’s analytic mass loss and structural evolution prescriptions are described in Sec. II.1. HJ15 and SatGen do not consider asphericity of halos. In this work, we adapt HJ15’s morphology metric to classify the morphology of the tidal debris that would result from a given satellite generated by SatGen.

### II.5 StreamGen Validation

We next validate the procedure described in the previous section by running N-body simulations of satellite galaxy mergers, applying the StreamGen morphology metric. The goal is to test the implementation of the StreamGen pipeline by inspecting the debris from N-body simulations and assessing whether its visual morphology agrees with the metric’s stream-like or shell-like classification. This validation tests the entire calculation of the StreamGen morphology metric assignment detailed in Sec. II.3, except we do not sample satellite particles, as we have full particle information in the N-body simulations, and we calculate the metric at most recent pericenter instead of p300. It is important to stress that we simulate similar galaxies but do not recreate exact SatGen mergers. We test the StreamGen morphology metric’s ability to accurately classify debris structures.

Using GALIC [133], we initialize a host galaxy with $M_{\mathrm{vir}}=5.03\times 10^{11}~M_{\odot}$ and $M_{*}=2.29\times 10^{10}~M_{\odot}$ , as well as a massive, luminous satellite with $M_{\mathrm{vir}}=9.2\times 10^{9}~M_{\odot}$ and $M_{*}=2.34\times 10^{6}~M_{\odot}$ . The satellite and host galaxies have dark matter halos and stellar bulges defined by Hernquist profiles; the host galaxy additionally contains an exponential stellar disk. GALIC creates a random N-body realization of the particle positions and iteratively adjusts the velocities until the galaxy stabilizes (i.e. the code finds a stationary solution of the collisionless Boltzmann equation). Both the satellite and host have a stellar and dark matter particle resolution of $320~M_{\odot}$ . However, to minimize computation time, we use agama to create a multipole potential of the GALIC host [124] and merge the N-body satellite into it. To create a variety of different merger configurations, we scan over a number of initial positions and velocities for the satellite, where each coordinate has a value in our chosen range of $[-100,100]$ kpc or km/s, respectively. We scan over the entire range to get a sample of stream-like and shell-like debris, but it is good to note that not all satellites within this range merge into the host. Then, we integrate the satellite orbit in the static host potential using agama for 13 Gyr. We apply the StreamGen morphology metric to the debris at its most recent pericenter, using $E_{\rm orb}$ , $L_{\rm orb}$ , $\Phi$ , $r_{\mathrm{apo}}$ , $r_{\mathrm{peri}}$ , $T_{r}$ , $\Delta\psi$ , and $\alpha_{r}$ , as defined in Sec. II.2.

We plot a selection of the results from these N-body simulations in Fig. 4. The left-most plot is structured in the same way as Fig. 3. The eight plots to the right show a sample of different satellite mergers that yield different stellar debris configurations, color-coded to match points in the left-hand plot. Stellar debris is displayed at most recent pericenter, viewed along the axis perpendicular to the satellite’s orbit at this point in time. The number in the upper right-hand corner of each of the smaller panels is the value of the morphology metric. Debris that visually appear stream-like have morphology metric values that are $<1$ . Stellar debris with the largest metric values are clearly not stream-like. There is an intermediate regime, where the morphology metric is ${\sim}\,1$ , in which the debris could be considered to be neither stream- or shell-like, but somewhere in between. Finally, there exist some satellites, such as the satellite colored brown, which are identified to be stream-like or shell-like, but visually are difficult to classify. We investigate this uncertainty further in Appendix A. We conclude that StreamGen can accurately separate very stream-like debris from debris that is distinctly not stream-like, with uncertainty in the intermediate regime. Appendix A explores the impact of the classification uncertainty on our final conclusions, demonstrating that the effect is negligible. It is good to note that “stream,” “shell,” and even “intact” are approximate boundaries; there is always inherent uncertainty in this classification, in simulations and observation.

## III Results

This work aims to understand how the properties of the host galaxy affect the abundance and orbital distribution of tidal debris. We present populations of tidally-disrupting satellites across ${\sim}\,1500$ SatGen host galaxies and discuss how the orbital properties of the satellites change as a function of host halo mass, disk mass, the ratio of disk scale radius to scale height, and baryonic feedback model. While it is likely that some of these modified parameters are correlated with each other, it is useful to gain intuition for how debris populations change as each of these host galaxy parameters is varied individually.

The corresponding shaded region indicates the $1\sigma$ scatter for each distribution. The debris behaves in predictable ways: satellites accreted at late times are largely intact today, while stream- and shell-like debris arise from satellites that accreted earlier. Current best estimates of the Milky Way’s mass lie in the range of $[0.5$ – $2.5]\times 10^{12}~M_{\odot}$ ( $[10^{11.7},10^{12.4}]$ ); see [125, 10] for recent reviews. The Milky Way’s disk mass is estimated in the range of $[3.5\pm 1]\times 10^{10}~M_{\odot}$ , leading to a disk mass fraction that ranges from $[0.01,0.09]$ [9]. According to [9], the scale height of the thin disk is $300\pm 50$ pc, and the scale length is $2.6\pm 0.5$ kpc, usually assuming that the density of the disk decreases as an exponential function of radius (and height in the case of the smooth double exponential disk model).77 7 The MN density profile for the disk used in this work is derived directly from the gravitational potential of the host, making it convenient for dynamical studies. However, this means that the scale radius and scale height calculated from observations are only approximate to the scale radius, $a$ , and scale height, $b$ , of the MN disk. Studying the effect of the specific disk model on tidal effects is worthwhile, but is not done in this work. This places the range of the ratio of disk scale radius to disk scale height to be between $\sim 6$ –12.

As a baseline for comparison, we define a fiducial model with host galaxies that are approximately Milky Way-mass $M_{\mathrm{vir}}\in[10^{11.5},10^{12.5}]~M_{\odot}$ , have a disk mass fraction of 0.05 times the host mass, a disk radius-to-height ratio of 25 (i.e. quite flat), and a bursty model of feedback tuned to the NIHAO simulations. Note that in this work, we do not attempt to exactly model the Milky Way but rather investigate how variations in model parameters around Milky Way estimates can affect the population of tidal debris. Section III.1 describes the substructure and orbital distribution for satellites in this fiducial model. Then, Sec. III.2 shows how these abundances and distributions change as we vary the model parameters.

### III.1 Fiducial Model

In this subsection, we examine the properties of intact satellites, as well as stream-like and shell-like debris, across the fiducial suite. To start, we investigate the survival of satellite galaxies by considering the distribution of accretion times for intact satellites compared to those undergoing stream-like or shell-like disruption—see Fig. 5. The stream-like and shell-like debris included in this figure are identified at p300, the time in a satellite’s orbit when the morphology metric is assigned. For the purposes of this analysis, we consider the morphology assigned at this point to be representative of the dominant structure of the debris at $z=0$ , as described in Sec. II.3. For each separate population shown in Fig. 5, the solid line denotes the median across the different host galaxy distributions, evaluated at a given lookback time; the shaded region corresponds to the $1\sigma$ scatter of the distributions. The purple, blue, orange, and grey colors correspond respectively to intact satellites, stream-like debris, shell-like debris, and satellites that have a pericenter $<4$ kpc. Satellites that are accreted at late times are typically still intact at $z=0$ , as they have not had time to undergo significant disruption. Accordingly, those that result in stream-like debris at the present day typically accreted earlier, with the distributions peaking at a median value of $\sim 8$ –9 Gyr. Shell-like structures are subdominant at all lookback times. One of the key results of Fig. 5—which will be a major theme in the ensuing discussion—is the large spread observed for all populations, which highlights the significant halo-to-halo variance in debris morphology across the SatGen galaxies.

*Figure 7: The median distributions of $r_{\mathrm{peri}}$ , $r_{\mathrm{apo}}$ , and eccentricity for intact satellites (purple), stream-like debris (blue), and shell-like debris (orange) for all galaxies in the fiducial model. The vertical line on each bar shows the $1\sigma$ spread across all galaxies. Stream-like and shell-like debris are largely associated with satellites on high-eccentricity orbits with pericenters of 0–20 kpc and apocenters in the range of 0–120 kpc.*

We emphasize that the shell-like and stream-like debris included in Fig. 5 have progenitor satellites with pericenters greater than 4 kpc. Recall that this cut is put in place to mitigate numerical issues for orbits passing near the center of the host. Satellites with pericenters smaller than 4 kpc will be significantly disrupted by strong tidal forces in the inner regions of the halo and are unlikely to form coherent streams [43]. We do not explicitly calculate the morphologies of these satellites, so we categorize them separately, but because of intense tidal processing in the inner regions of the halo, we expect most to be shell-like or fully phase mixed [62]. The results from Fig. 5 (grey line/band) suggest that there may be additional contributions to the total number of shell-like debris (and possibly some stream-like debris) in each galaxy of the suite, beyond what is included in our shell-like and stream-like classification.

The stellar mass distribution function of satellite galaxies provides insights into satellite survival rates and a point of comparison between observations and simulations. The bar charts in Fig. 6 show the median cumulative peak stellar mass distribution of satellites which remain intact (purple), as well as those which become stream-like (blue) and shell-like (orange). [114] performed a detailed study of pericenter and apocenter distributions for stream-like debris in the FIRE simulations [54, 55, 56, 74]. They found a potential discrepancy between simulations and observations: the stream-like debris identified in 13 Milky Way analogs consistently had higher $r_{\mathrm{peri}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{apo}}$ than observed streams in the Milky Way. StreamGen provides an opportunity to compare these results against a larger sample of semi-analytically modelled Milky Way hosts. Our fiducial model is roughly FIRE-like in terms of host mass range: the fiducial model hosts have $M_{\mathrm{vir}}\in[10^{11.5},10^{12.5}]$ , and the FIRE galaxies exist in the mid-high end of this range. FIRE galaxies have thin disks with scale lengths in the range of 3–5 kpc and scale heights around 200–500 pc [79, 32, 108]. This places the range of the ratio of disk scale radius to scale height to be between ${\sim}\,6$ – $15$ . The fiducial model has a flatter disk than the FIRE galaxies, with a disk scale radius to scale height of 25. Finally, the fiducial model has feedback tuned to the burstier feedback of the NIHAO simulations [118, 42], characterized by intermittent, intense supernovae outflows. This burstier feedback model is similar—though not the same in detail—to the FIRE feedback prescription. Selecting for satellites with $M_{*}>5\times 10^{5}~M_{\odot}$ as done in [114], we find good agreement with the abundance of StreamGen stream-like debris in the fiducial model to the FIRE stream-like debris, especially considering the halo-to-halo variance. However, we find stream-like debris that exist at $r_{\mathrm{apo}}<50$ kpc and $r_{\mathrm{peri}}<20$ kpc, lower than what was found in FIRE. Whether or not these differences could be attributed to differences the modeling of host properties will be discussed in Sec. IV.
